title: How would you manage Git branching across a development team (feature branching, PR flow, hotfix branches)?
shortTitle: Git branching across a development team — feature branches, PR flow, hotfix branches

s1_definition.profdef: A Git branching strategy is an agreed set of conventions for how a team creates, reviews, and merges branches so that many developers can work in parallel without breaking the shared mainline. A common approach is trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches: each developer branches off main, works on one isolated change, opens a pull request for review and automated checks, and merges back quickly. Hotfix branches are short branches cut from a production release to fix an urgent bug and merged back into both the release and main.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of main as the official, always-correct master ledger of National Bank of India that every branch relies on. A feature branch is like a teller taking a photocopy of the ledger to draft a set of changes privately, so their work-in-progress never corrupts the real ledger. A pull request is submitting that draft to a supervisor who checks it line by line before it is merged into the master ledger. A hotfix branch is an emergency correction — a fraud is detected in the live ledger, so a senior officer makes a tightly scoped fix straight on a copy of the current official version, applies it immediately, and then makes sure the same correction is also written into the ongoing drafts so it is never lost.
s1_definition.oneliner: Branch short-lived features off main, merge them back through reviewed pull requests, and cut hotfix branches from production for urgent fixes that flow back into main.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Git branching strategy is an agreed set of conventions for how a team creates, reviews, and merges branches so that many developers can work in parallel without breaking the shared mainline. A common approach is trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches: each developer branches off main, works on one isolated change, opens a pull request for review and automated checks, and merges back quickly. Hotfix branches are short branches cut from a production release to fix an urgent bug and merged back into both the release and main.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of main as the official, always-correct master ledger of National Bank of India that every branch relies on. A feature branch is like a teller taking a photocopy of the ledger to draft a set of changes privately, so their work-in-progress never corrupts the real ledger. A pull request is submitting that draft to a supervisor who checks it line by line before it is merged into the master ledger. A hotfix branch is an emergency correction — a fraud is detected in the live ledger, so a senior officer makes a tightly scoped fix straight on a copy of the current official version, applies it immediately, and then makes sure the same correction is also written into the ongoing drafts so it is never lost.

**One line to remember:** Branch short-lived features off main, merge them back through reviewed pull requests, and cut hotfix branches from production for urgent fixes that flow back into main.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is a protected main branch. Main is the single source of truth, it must always be releasable, and nobody pushes to it directly. You enforce this with branch protection rules: require a pull request, require at least one approving review, and require status checks like build and tests to pass before merge. For a bank this is non-negotiable, because main is what gets deployed to production where customer money lives.

The everyday workflow is feature branching. When a developer starts work, they create a new branch off the latest main, named descriptively like feature/loan-interest-calculation or bugfix/transfer-rounding. They commit their work there in isolation, so their incomplete code never touches main and never blocks teammates. The strong recommendation is to keep these branches short-lived — hours or a few days, not weeks — because a long-lived branch drifts far from main and produces painful merge conflicts. This short-lived feature-branch style is often called trunk-based development.

The pull request flow is how work gets reviewed and merged. The developer pushes the branch and opens a pull request targeting main. This triggers two things: automated continuous integration runs the build, unit tests, and often static analysis and security scans; and human reviewers read the diff and comment. The PR is a conversation — reviewers ask questions, request changes, and the developer pushes more commits until approved. Only when checks pass and the required approvals are in does the PR merge. This gives you peer review, an audit trail of who approved what, and a gate that stops broken code reaching main.

Keeping feature branches current matters. While a developer works, main moves on as teammates merge their PRs. The developer regularly updates their branch from main — either by merging main in or by rebasing onto main — so conflicts are resolved in small pieces early rather than as one huge conflict at the end. Smaller, more frequent integration is always less painful.

Hotfix branches handle production emergencies. Suppose a critical bug is found in the live release — say transfers are being double-counted. You cannot wait for the normal feature cycle. You cut a hotfix branch directly from the production release point, make the smallest possible fix, get an expedited review, and deploy it fast. Crucially, you then merge that same fix back into main so the bug does not reappear in the next normal release. If the team uses a separate long-lived release branch, the hotfix merges into both the release branch and main.

A few senior-level nuances tie it together. Merge strategy matters: squash-and-merge collapses a feature branch into one clean commit on main, which keeps history readable, while a merge commit preserves the full branch history. Naming conventions and linking commits to ticket numbers make the history traceable, which auditors love. And for very large teams, feature flags let you merge incomplete features to main safely behind a switch, avoiding long-lived branches entirely. The overarching principle is: main always works, branches are short-lived and isolated, every change is reviewed, and urgent production fixes have a fast, well-defined path that still ends up back in main.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a payments repository worked on by eight engineers. The team needs a branching discipline that lets everyone move fast without breaking production.

Problem 1 — early on, engineers pushed directly to main, and one incomplete change broke the build for the whole team for half a day. This is exactly why main must be protected and why work happens on isolated feature branches merged only through reviewed pull requests.

Problem 2 — an engineer kept a branch alive for three weeks, and merging it back caused dozens of conflicts that took two days to untangle. This is exactly why branches must be short-lived and regularly updated from main, keeping integration small and continuous.

Problem 3 — a critical bug double-charged customers in the live release. Waiting for the normal cycle was unacceptable. This is exactly what a hotfix branch is for — a tiny, fast, reviewed fix cut from production, deployed immediately, then merged back into main so it never regresses.

The mini-project is a concrete git command walkthrough for one feature (adding an interest calculation) and one hotfix (a double-charge bug), plus a small Java class that the feature adds and the hotfix corrects, so the branching story maps onto real code.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: engineer A develops an interest-calculation feature while, in parallel, a double-charge bug is found in the live v1.4.0 release and must be hotfixed.

Step 1: Engineer A updates main, creates feature/loan-interest-calculation off it, and adds InterestCalculator plus tests in small commits. This work is isolated — main is untouched and teammates are unblocked.

Step 2: While A works, two other PRs merge into main. A runs git fetch and rebases the feature branch onto the new main, resolving one small conflict immediately rather than a giant one later.

Step 3: A pushes the branch and opens a pull request targeting main. CI runs the build and tests, which pass, and a reviewer reads the diff, asks for a clearer method name, and A pushes one more commit. With green CI and an approval, the PR is squash-merged into main as a single clean commit.

Step 4: Meanwhile, operations reports that v1.4.0 double-charges interest on retried requests. A separate engineer cuts hotfix/double-charge-fix directly from the v1.4.0 tag, so the fix is based on exactly what is in production, not on in-progress work.

Step 5: The engineer makes the minimal idempotency fix, gets an expedited review, tags v1.4.1, and deploys it to production fast. Customers stop being double-charged.

Step 6: Crucially, the engineer merges the same hotfix commit back into main. Now the fix exists in both production and the mainline, so the next normal release cannot reintroduce the bug. Both the feature and the hotfix are now part of main.

```

Oct 25, 2026 02:45:40 AM INFO: PR #318 CI green, 1 approval -> squash-merged to main
Oct 25, 2026 02:50:03 AM SEVERE: PROD v1.4.0 double-charge detected
Oct 25, 2026 02:55:22 AM INFO: hotfix/double-charge-fix cut from tag v1.4.0
Oct 25, 2026 03:05:10 AM INFO: v1.4.1 deployed; hotfix merged back into main
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  main (protected, always releasable)
    │
    ├── git checkout -b feature/loan-interest-calculation
    │      │ commit, commit
    │      │ rebase onto origin/main  (stay current)
    │      │ push -> Pull Request
    │      │    ├─ CI: build + tests ✓
    │      │    └─ review: 1 approval ✓
    │      ▼ squash-merge
    │   main (now has feature) ◀───────────────┐
    │                                           │
    │   PROD v1.4.0 ── double-charge bug ──┐    │
    │                                       ▼    │
    └── git checkout -b hotfix/... v1.4.0       │
           │ minimal fix + expedited review     │
           │ tag v1.4.1 -> deploy to prod        │
           └── merge hotfix BACK into main ──────┘
               (fix lives in prod AND main -> no regression)
```

```
                                           \  tag v1.4.1 -> prod
                                            \

  ── State Diagram: a Pull Request ──────────────────────────

  [OPEN] ──CI runs──→ [CHECKS_PENDING] ──green + approved──→ [MERGEABLE]
     │                      │ CI red / changes requested          │ merge
     │                      ▼                                     ▼
     │                 [BLOCKED] ──push fixes──→ [CHECKS_PENDING]  [MERGED]
     └── closed without merge ──→ [CLOSED]

  ── Call Chain (feature -> main) ───────────────────────────

  1. git checkout -b feature/... main
  2. commit work (small, ticketed)
  3. git rebase origin/main         (stay current)
  4. git push -> open PR
  5. CI: build + test + scan        (gate)
  6. review approval                (gate)
  7. squash-merge -> main ; delete branch
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The way I manage Git branching across a team starts with a protected main branch that is the single source of truth and must always be releasable. Nobody pushes to main directly; I enforce branch protection rules that require a pull request, at least one approving review, and passing CI checks before any merge. For a bank this is non-negotiable, because main is what reaches production where customer money lives.

The everyday workflow is short-lived feature branching, which is essentially trunk-based development. A developer branches off the latest main with a descriptive name like feature slash loan-interest-calculation, commits their work in isolation so incomplete code never blocks teammates, and keeps the branch short — hours or a few days, not weeks. Long-lived branches drift from main and cause painful conflicts, so I have developers regularly update their branch from main, resolving small conflicts early instead of one giant conflict at the end.

Work reaches main through the pull request flow. The developer pushes the branch and opens a PR, which triggers automated continuous integration — build, tests, static analysis, security scans — and human review. The PR is a conversation until it is approved, and only with green checks and the required approvals does it merge. I usually squash-merge so main's history stays clean and readable, and I link commits to ticket numbers so the history is traceable, which auditors value.

Hotfixes get a fast, well-defined path. When a critical bug hits the live release — for example payments double-charging on a retry — I cut a hotfix branch directly from the production release tag so the fix is based on exactly what is running, make the smallest possible change, get an expedited review, and deploy immediately. The crucial step is merging that same fix back into main so the bug never regresses in the next normal release. At National Bank of India this discipline — protected trunk, short-lived reviewed feature branches, and a fast hotfix path that always flows back to main — let eight engineers work in parallel on the payments service without ever breaking production.
